# Challenges with Missing Data {#sec-intro}

In most statistical and machine learning literature, datasets are assumed to be complete. For instance, in case of tabular data, it is assumed that all features are observed for each sample. Similarly, in the case of multivariate time-series data, it is often assumed that all features for each sample are measured at the same time points. In practice however, datasets are often *incomplete*, with some features unobserved for certain samples, or *fragmented* in case of time-series data, with observations or features missing at different time points across samples.
<!--Introduce time-series data, so that you can define the terms 'irregular' and 'fragmented' in relation to that, in layman's terms. Add the biological example of patients to explain and define these words-->
<!--More details - heterogenous samples at different timepoints, missing labels, etc.Summarise all the motivations. don't go into concrete examples here, put it in the motivation-->

A similar issue is label missingness, which has given rise to the field of semi-supervised learning. Label missingness refers to the scenario where only some samples in the dataset are labeled. However, approaches to semi-supervised learning often assume similar distribution of the missing labels as the available labels, which is often not reflected in real world scenarios. An example for this is the task of anomaly detection, where often only some positive samples are labeled and the unlabeled part of the dataset consists overwhelmingly of non-anomalous samples.

In this chapter, I will introduce the different types of missingness that has been proposed in the literature, as well as propose a new classification of missingness based on a different perspective. I will also discuss how the semi-supervised setting can be viewed as a special case of missing data, and how it can be incorporated into the overall missingness framework.

## Motivation for dealing with missingness

### Missing data in the real-world setting and Challenges - Missing attributes <!-- mention 'privacy issues' in the conclusion of thesis instead of the introduction-->

A common example of incomplete and fragmented data in the biomedical data is electronic health records. Patients usually have different lengths of stay in a hospital, and are prescribed different medical tests depending on their symptoms. Compiling this data into a single dataset usually results in extensive missingness across features and time points, resulting in an incomplete, fragmented and sparse data structure. For example, in @boneDensityData the collected dataset records longitudinal bone density data of 423 individuals from 9-26 years of age. Although measurements for all individuals span almost 18 years of age, measurements were actually made for each individual at most four times, typically across less than 5 years. This causes the dataset to be highly fragmented in the time domain. Similarly, a prominent real-life benchmark in multivariate time series research is the Beijing Multi-Site Air Quality dataset [@airQualityData], which exhibits sporadic missing features and irregular temporal alignment across monitoring locations.

### History of simple unsupervised imputation - constants, measures of central tendency, extremums, etc.
<!--mention in title that it's tabular data-->

*Imputation* is defined as the procedure of filling in missing or null values in a dataset with substituted values. Some simple structured approaches to imputation are:


* Constant - Also known as *padding*, this method of imputation simply fills in the missing values with a constant, often 0.
* Statistical measures of central tendency - Measures of central tendency like the mean, median, or mode are often used to fill in missing values in tabular data in order to preserve the marginal statistical properties of the features. However, this method disregards the interdependencies between the features.
* Last Observation Carried Forward - Another simple imputation method that's usually applied to time series data is to simply fill in the missing values with the last observed value for that particular feature. This however assumes that regime change and concept drift have not occurred in the timesteps between that last observed value and the current missing values, as well as the aforementioned ignoring of inter-variable statistical dependencies.
* Variance Minimization - Consider a set of samples for different groups. Using the classical ANOVA structure, data can be imputed by minimizing the group-wise variances, which conditions the imputed values on the targets in order to preserve group-wise statistical properties.
* Nearest Neighbor Imputation - If group-wise labels are unavailable, another approach is to impute the values using the top-K nearest neighbors with available features for each sample with missing features.
* Iterative Imputation[@mice] - This approach models imputation as a round-robin regression problem. At each step, one feature with missing values is selected as the target, and the rest of the variables are selected as regressors. The model fits a regression model on the available values as uses its predictions to fill in the missing values. This is done for each feature over several steps until all the missing feature values have been filled out.
* Generative models - Generative models can be modified to also perform imputation by conditioning the generated values upon the observed values for each feature and each sample. This usually involves masking some of the observed values and training a model to generate them based on the unmasked values. This model is then used to also generate the missing values. Some examples of this include GAN based models (GAIN [@gain]), diffusion-based models (CSDI [@csdi]).

### Longitudinal data and missing data

Time-series data needs to consider an additional dimension. Not only do the imputed values need to preserve feature-wise interdependencies to remain unbiased, they also have to consider correlations across time. For this reason, the simplest and most widely used imputation method for time-series data is \acr{LOCF}, which involves simply copying over the most recently observed value for each feature to fill in the missing values. The assumptions here is that systems evolve slowly and are strongly autocorrelated with the recent past, so the current value for a feature should not diverge significantly from the last observed value. However, these assumptions can be violated in cases where there is a change in the data distribution between the current missing time point and the last observed time point (also known as concept drift[@conceptDrift] in continual learning).

A slightly more advanced approach to imputation in longitudinal data is matrix/tensor factorization or completion. The idea is to find values for the missing entries such that the rank of the filled in matrix/tensor is minimized. In the case of matrix completion, @matrixCompletionProof showed that if the number of sampled entries was high enough, then most matrices can be perfectly recovered by solving a simple convex optimization problem. Recent work has extended these results to a certain decomposition of 3-way tensors[@tensorCompletionProof], but these results are not as strong as there are many different definitions of the rank of a tensor. @btf shows an example of this type of approach.

Modern approaches to time-series imputation uses generative models. One of the most well-known modern methods is known as CSDI[@csdi], where some of the observed values are masked and a diffusion model is trained to predict the masked values. The same model can then be used to predict the missing values. Similar approaches can be designed for other generative models like \acr{VAE} models[@gpVae] or \acr{GAN} models[@gain]

## Notation

### Mathematical formulation

Throughout this thesis, I will use the standardized notation encouraged by most machine learning conferences. Italicized letters will indicate deterministic quantities. Normal small letters indicate numbers ($x,y,t$), bold small letters indicate vectors ($\vx,\vy,\vt$), bold capital letters indicate matrices ($\mX,\mY,\mT$), capital letters in sans-serif fonts indicate tensors $(\tX,\tY,\tT)$ and blackboard bold capital letters indicate sets ($\sX,\sY,\sT$) (with the exception of $\E$ and $\P$ which are defined below). The non-italicized versions of these indicate random quatities; random variables are $\rx,\ry,\rt$, random vectors are $\rvx,\rvy,\rvt$ and random matrices are $\rmX,\rmY,\rmT$. Elements of higher order arrays like vectors, matrices, and higher order tensors are denoted by regular versions of the bold letters with subscripts: $\evx_1,\emX_{11},\etX_{111},\ervx_1,\ermX_{11}$, etc. For a matrix $\mX$, $\mX_{i,:}$ and $\mX_{:,i}$ will denote the $i^{th}$ row and column respectively.

When two random variables $\rx$ and $\ry$ are independent, I will denote that as $\rx\independent\ry$.

I will denote the vectorization of a matrix $\mX$, which means stacking the columns of the matrix sequentially, as
$$\vec(\mX)=[\mX_{:,1}^\trans\quad\mX_{:,2}^\trans\quad\cdots\quad\mX_{:,n}^\trans]^\trans$$
The determinant of a matrix $\mA$ will be denoted by $|\mA|$, and Kronecker product of two matrices $\mA_{m\times n}$ and $\mB_{p\times q}$ is an $mp\times nq$ matrix defined as
$$
\mA\kron\mB\deff\begin{bmatrix}
\emA_{11}\mB &\emA_{12}\mB&\cdots\emA_{1n}\mB\\
\emA_{21}\mB &\emA_{22}\mB&\cdots\emA_{2n}\mB\\
\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\
\emA_{m1}\mB &\emA_{m2}\mB&\cdots\emA_{mn}\mB\\
\end{bmatrix}
$$
The generalized pseudo-inverse [@pseudoinverse, pp. 20] of a matrix $\mA$ will be denoted by $\mA^-$, which simply indicates that $\mA\mA^-\mA=\mA$. It should be clear that the choice of $\mA^-$ is not unique for a singular matrix $\mA$, *i.e.* if $|\mA|=0$. In cases where a unique choice is necessary, I will use the Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse [@penrosePseudoinverse] $\mA^+$, which is defined by the following properties:
$$\mA\mA^+\mA=\mA\qquad\mA^+\mA\mA^+=\mA^+\qquad(\mA\mA^+)^*=\mA\mA^+\qquad(\mA^+\mA)^*=\mA^+\mA$$.

I will denote the probability of an event $E$ as $\P(E)$, expectation of a random variable $\rx$ as $\E[\rx]$, its variance as $\Var(\rx)$, and its covariance with another random variable $\ry$ as $\Cov(\rx,\ry)$. I will denote the variance-covariance matrix of a random vector $\rvx$ as $\Var(\rvx)$. For a matrix $\mSigma$, $\norm{\rvx}_\mSigma$ will denote the Mahalanobis norm [@mahalanobisDistance] of $\rvx$ with covariance $\mSigma$, defined as $\norm{\rvx}_\mSigma\deff\rvx^\trans\mSigma^-\rvx$.

I will also denote the KL divergence of 2 distributions $P$ and $Q$ over the support $\sX$ as
$$\KL(P||Q)\deff\int_{x\in\sX}P(x)\log\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}dx$$
The Cartesian product of two sets $\sA$ and $\sB$ will be denoted by $\sA\times\sB$.

## Problem Formulation (Add more discussion about the definitions, to motivate to non-experts)

I will adopt notation similar to @hyperimpute for the problem formulation and denote missing values as `NaN`. Let $\rvx\in \sX=(\sX_1\times\ldots\sX_D)$ be a D-dimensional random vector. The entries of this random vector can be continuous ($\sX_d=\R$) or categorical ($\sX_d=\{1,\ldots,K_d\}$) random variables, for $d\in\{1,\ldots,D\}$. We do not have complete observational access to $\rvx$; instead our observation is mediated by a random masking vector $\rvm\in\{0,1\}^D$. If $\ervm_d=1$, then $\ervx_d$ is observed. Assume that $\rvm$ follows a distribution $\pmask$, and the data $\rvx$ follows a distribution $\pdata$. <!--Say there are $N$ samples, and index everything by $i$, where $i$ is the index of the sample-->

## Types of missingness

Classical literature mainly distinguishes three main missingness mechanisms depending on the relationship between the probability of missingness with the observed and unobserved data [@typesOfMissingness]. These can be distinguished based on the form and properties of $\pmask$.

### \acr{MCAR}

\acr{MCAR} is a missingness mechanism where the probability of missingness is independent of the observed and unobserved data. In other words, the missingness is completely random and does not depend on any of the observed or unobserved data. This is equivalent to the statement that $\rvx\independent\rvm$. This also indicates that each component of $\vm, m_i$, is an independent Bernoulli random variable with probability $p_i$ independent of $\vx$.

::: {#exm-MCAR}

@mcarExample presents an example of a \acr{MCAR} dataset collected via a questionaire. Some data is missing due to non-response to some questions, and Little's \acr{MCAR} test[@littleMCARTest] shows that the choice to not answer certain questions is taken completely at random.
:::

### \acr{MAR}

The missingness mechanism \acr{MAR} indicates that the probability of missingness depends only on the observed values. In more technicality, let $\rvx$ and $\rvm$ be partitoned as $\{\rvx_1,\rvx_2\}$ and $\{\rvm_1,\rvm_2\}$ respectively, such that $\rvx_1$ is always observed, that is, $\rvm_1=\mathbf{1}$. Then, $\rvx$ is said to be \acr{MAR} if $\pmask$ depends only on $\rvx_1$.

::: {#rem-logisticMAR}

# Logistic Model for MAR

A simple model of \acr{MAR} data, and one I will use in this thesis to demonstrate and evaluate imputation methods on the \acr{MAR} scenario, is
$$
\pmask(\rvm_2\mid\rvx_1)=\frac{1}{1+\exp(-\rmW\rvx_1)},
$${#eq-MAR}
where $\rmW$ is a random matrix.

:::

::: {#exm-MAR}

@marExample illustrates a scenario in which missing data in \acr{EHRs} follow the \acr{MAR} mechanism. Using data from the Flatiron Health database, the authors investigate the effect of \acr{Hgb} levels on real-world overall survival across several tumor types. They first apply Little's \acr{MCAR} test and, when the null hypothesis is rejected, train a random-forest classifier to predict \acr{Hgb} missingness from the other observed covariates, evaluating its performance using \acr{AUROC}. For patients with multiple myeloma, functional status (ECOG performance score at the index date) was found to be a strong predictor of \acr{Hgb} missingness. This is consistent with the clinical practice of drawing blood less frequently from highly functional patients without signs of illness. Thus, the probability of \acr{Hgb} missingness depends on observed variables, consistent with an \acr{MAR} mechanism.

<!--@marExample show a scenario where missing data in \acr{EHRs} follows the \acr{MAR} mechanism. Data is derived from the Flatiron Health database, the impact of \acr{Hgb} levels on real-world overall survival across several tumor types is analyzed. In order to test for the missigness mechanism, the authors first perform Little's \acr{MCAR} test. If the null hypothesis is rejected, they fit a random-forest based classifier model to predict missingness of \acr{Hgb} values based on the other covariates, and compute the \acr{AUROC} score of the trained model. In the case of patiens diagnosed with multiple myeloma, it was seen that functional activity levels (ECOG performance scores at index date) are a strong predictor of the missingness of \acr{Hgb} values, which can be explained by the fact that medical practitioners are unlikely to draw blood if patient is highly functional and shows no signs of illness. :::

### \acr{MNAR}

If data is missing by the \acr{MNAR} mechanism, the probability of missingness depends both on the observed and the unobserved data. Mathematically, $\pmask$ depends on all elements of $\rvx$. A model similar to @eq-MAR can be developed for this scenario, but a much simpler model that still allows us to evaluate methods and derive theoretical guarantees is Gaussian self-masking
$$
\pmask(\ervm_i\mid\ervx_i) = K_i\exp(-\frac{(\ervx_i-\tilde{\mu}_i)^2}{2\tilde{\sigma}_i^2})
$$
where $\tilde{\mu}_i$ and $\tilde{\sigma}_i^2$ are the mean and variance of the observed values of the $i^\text{th}$ components of $\rvx$, and $0<K_i\leq 1$ is a scaling factor.

::: {#rem-gaussianSelfMasking}
# Gaussian Self-Masking
This model encodes dependence only on the (possibly) missing value. However, the case where missingness depends on the observed values is already considered under the \acr{MAR} mechanism, so in this thesis, Gaussian self-masking will be the primary model for \acr{MNAR} data.
:::

::: {#exm-MNAR}

@mnarExample presents a questionnaire dataset shown to exhibit \acr{MNAR} missingness. Participants who left certain questions unanswered received reminders, recovering approximately 50% of the missing responses. A logistic regression model was then used to assess whether the observed covariates and the recovered responses predicted missingness. Since the recovered responses were statistically significant predictors, the missingness mechanism was concluded to be \acr{MNAR}.

:::

## Semi-Supervised Learning as a Missing Value Problem

Semi-supervised learning is a learning task where only some of the samples are labeled with target values. Let the samples $\mX:=\{\vx_i\}_{i\in[n]}$ be divided into two parts: $\mX_l:=(\vx_i)_{i\in[l]}$, for which labels $\vy=(y_i)_\{y_i\}_{i\in[l]}$ are available, and $\mX_u:=\{y_i\}_{i\in\{[n]\setminus[l]\}}$, for which labels are unavailable.
